subject: chemistry
question_text: Define heat capacity. What are Cp and Cv? Show that Cp − Cv = R.

verification.note: Unit 6 Thermodynamics is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.73-75), which prints the question, its star rank and a model answer. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. This chapter has NO Long Answer section in the book, so no 8-mark form is invented. The 1+1+1+1 mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. CUTS: the book asks this content at two lengths — SAQ 4 asks the definition plus the derivation (4 marks), and VSAQ 11 asks only the relation between Cp and Cv (2 marks) — so this one file carries both cuts of one step list. The book derives the relation by differentiating H = E + PV; this card uses the equivalent NCERT algebra route with ΔT, which needs no calculus.

steps.label: Heat capacity defined
lines: Heat capacity C of a system is the amount
of heat required to raise its temperature
steps.why: The derivation compares two heat capacities, so the answer must first state what a heat capacity is.
common_mistakes: Defining it per gram (specific heat capacity) or per mole (molar heat capacity) when the plain definition is asked.
steps.memory_tip: Heat capacity answers one question: how much heat for one degree?
steps.margin_note: One sentence and the defining equation.

steps.label: Cp and Cv
lines: Cp = heat capacity at constant pressure.
Cv = heat capacity at constant volume.
For one mole of a gas these are the molar
steps.why: A gas can be heated with its volume held fixed or its pressure held fixed, and the two ways need different amounts of heat — at constant pressure part of the heat becomes expansion work.
common_mistakes: Swapping the two — p stands for pressure, v for volume.
Forgetting that Cp is larger than Cv for a gas.
steps.memory_tip: Cp is larger than Cv because at constant pressure part of the heat becomes expansion work.
steps.margin_note: Both meanings in words earn this mark.

steps.label: Derivation
lines: At constant volume:  qv = Cv ΔT = ΔU
At constant pressure: qp = Cp ΔT = ΔH
For one mole of an ideal gas, pV = RT, so

lines.text: ΔH = ΔU + Δ(pV) = ΔU + R ΔT

lines: Cp ΔT = Cv ΔT + R ΔT
steps.why: Enthalpy exceeds internal energy by pV, and for one mole of an ideal gas pV rises by R for every one-degree rise in temperature. The source book reaches the same result by differentiating H = E + PV with respect to T.
common_mistakes: Not stating one mole — for n moles the pV term is nRT and the relation reads Cp − Cv = nR in total heat capacities.
Skipping the pV = RT line, which is where the ideal gas enters.
steps.memory_tip: One mole, one degree: the extra heat needed at constant pressure is exactly R.
steps.margin_note: Each line follows from the one before; the pV = RT line must appear.

steps.label: The relation

lines.text: Cp − Cv = R  (one mole of an ideal gas)

lines: R is the universal gas constant,
steps.why: The difference between the two molar heat capacities of an ideal gas is the gas constant itself — this is the result the question asks for.
common_mistakes: Writing Cv − Cp = R. Cp is the larger one, so Cp − Cv is positive.
steps.memory_tip: The relation is a subtraction that leaves R: Cp minus Cv equals R.
steps.margin_note: Box this line. Adding the value of R shows the unit is known.

insider_note: Asked at two lengths: Section A wants only the relation, Section B wants the definition and the derivation. Check which section the paper puts it in before deciding how much to write.

cuts.label: 2-mark answer
cuts.question_text: Write the relation between Cp and Cv for an ideal gas.
cuts.note: VSAQ 11 asks only the relation: say what Cp and Cv are and box Cp − Cv = R. The definition and the derivation belong to the 4-mark form.
